## Q1
Match List I with List II on PERT and CPM concepts.

| List-I | List-II |
|---|---|
| A. PERT | I. used for non repetitive jobs |
| B. Optimistic time | II. Used for repetitive jobs |
| C. CPM | III. The shortest possible time to complete the activity if all goes well |
| D. Pessimistic time | IV. The longest time that an activity takes |

List I / List II: PERT and CPM project management concepts

## Q1 - Options
(A) A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I
(B) A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III
(C) A-I, B-III, C-II, D-II
(D) A-I, B-III, C-II, D-IV

## Q1 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Optimization: PERT/CPM & Integer Programming
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q72

Each project-management term matches its defining role.

- PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Technique) is used for non-repetitive, uncertain jobs such as research and development projects — A-I.
- Optimistic time is the shortest possible time to complete an activity if everything goes exactly as planned — B-III.
- CPM (Critical Path Method) is used for repetitive, well-understood jobs such as construction projects — C-II.
- Pessimistic time is the longest time an activity could take under unfavorable conditions — D-IV.

This gives the mapping A-I, B-III, C-II, D-IV.

- **A. A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I** — swaps PERT with optimistic time, and CPM's pairing with pessimistic time's pairing.
- **B. A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III** — swaps PERT with pessimistic time, and optimistic time with PERT's pairing.
- **C. A-I, B-III, C-II, D-II** — repeats "II" for both C and D, leaving pessimistic time without its correct "longest time" pairing.
- **D. A-I, B-III, C-II, D-IV** — correct, matches every pairing above.

## Q2
Consider the statements:

A. There does not exist a polynomial time algorithm to solve integer linear programming problem.<br>
B. Main focus of PERT is 'minimizing time'.

Choose the correct option about the statements A and B.

## Q2 - Options
(A) A is True; B is True
(B) A is True; B is False
(C) A is False; B is True
(D) A is False; B is False

## Q2 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Optimization: PERT/CPM & Integer Programming
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (11 Mar, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q76

Integer linear programming is NP-hard, so no polynomial time algorithm is known for it, which makes statement A true.

PERT and CPM are commonly distinguished in project management by their focus, with PERT built around estimating and managing uncertain activity durations to plan project time, so statement B's claim that PERT centers on time is also considered true.

Both statements are true.

## Q3
In PERT/CPM, the merge event represents \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ of two or more events.

## Q3 - Options
(A) splitting
(B) beginning
(C) completion
(D) joining

## Q3 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Optimization: PERT/CPM & Integer Programming
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2018 (20 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q65

In PERT and CPM project networks, a merge node represents the point where two or more incoming activities complete.

- A merge event occurs when multiple predecessor activities must finish before subsequent dependent activities can begin.
- It formally marks the joint completion of all incoming activity paths.
- A burst event represents the beginning of multiple activities from a single node.
- Therefore, completion is the standard term (Option C).
